1:
Chrysostom explains why the argument starts here at all. The new covenant had nothing bodily to show, no temple, no holy of holies, no priest in great apparel, and spiritual things do not draw the weak as visible ones do; so the writer begins from the priesthood and defines what a priest is before saying who his own is. The difficulty is real, since the figure he means to call a priest was not well-born, not of the priestly tribe, and never a priest on earth. Calvin sets out the definition in five clauses: priests were taken from men, acted not privately but for the whole people, came furnished with sacrifices rather than empty, were not exempt from human infirmity so that they might the more readily succour the distressed, and did not thrust themselves into the office. Barnes gives the setting: the Jews held the high priesthood essential to true religion, so it had to be shown that those who left Judaism had lost nothing by the change. Henry reads the first clause as implying three things at once: that man had sinned, that God would not admit him immediately, and that God was pleased to take one from among men by whom he might be approached.

On the two kinds of offering Clarke builds a scheme out of how God was regarded: as giver of all temporal good he received offerings acknowledging his bounty, as lawgiver and judge sacrifices making atonement, the first word covering every thank-offering and the second every victim whose blood was poured out. Ellicott narrows it to the ritual, taking the first term for the unbloody offerings of the Law and noting that the Day of Atonement is almost always in this writer's mind, on which day every offering alike had relation to sins. Clarke traces the taking from among men to the law requiring the high priest to come from his brethren. Robertson reduces the passage to two requirements, human sympathy and divine appointment, observes that the verb of offering is a present and so means offering from time to time, and adds the qualification the argument will turn on, that the sins offered for include the priest's own in every case but one. Wesley glosses the appointing as what was customary rather than what happened once, and the phrase about the things of God as bringing God near to men and men to God. Calvin denies that any of it licenses a continuing sacrifice, the reality having displaced the types.

The verb behind "have compassion" carries a philosophical history, and Robertson and Calvin recover it independently. Both explain that the Stoics held a wise man should be without passion altogether while the school opposed to them required a measured feeling instead, and that this word belongs to the second; Robertson adds that it is used elsewhere of a general's moderation toward a conquered people. Calvin doubts that the philosophical sense is quite what is wanted and prefers, on the lexicographers, the sense of being indulgent or forbearing. Clarke makes it bearing with each man in proportion to his ignorance and circumstances and, where punishment must fall, administering it in the gentlest manner; he notes one reputable manuscript reading "the weak" for "the ignorant," and grants that weakness excuses nobody who has the means of strength at hand. Ellicott observes that either apathy or undue severity would disqualify a man for the office. Robertson quotes a description of what the priest must bridle if he is to plead for sinners: his disgust at sensuality, his impatience at the fall that keeps recurring, his alienation from the hypocrite, his indignation at what he hears confessed. Both he and Wesley note that the priest wears his own weakness like a chain, and Barnes extends the argument to the ministry, chosen from among men because they are of like passions, sinners and dying.
3:
Ellicott ties the verse back to the one before it and fills in the ritual it assumes. The law of the Day of Atonement required of the high priest a sin-offering of a bullock and a burnt-offering of a ram for himself, and for the congregation a sin-offering of two goats with a burnt-offering of a ram; over his own offering he confessed first for himself and his household, then for the priests, while the people's sins were confessed over the goat sent into the wilderness. Barnes puts the consequence plainly, that the man needs the atonement he administers, and carries it forward to the ministry, whose members plead for their own salvation the merits of the blood they show to be indispensable for everyone else. Clarke makes the same point turn into a qualification: being himself a transgressor unable to keep the law in its spirituality, the priest is taught by his own offering to have a fellow feeling. Gill compresses it to five words about sinful infirmity. Robertson notices only that the preposition has changed from the one used two verses earlier, and that the two were interchangeable in the Greek of the period.

Clarke settles what the word rendered honour means, arguing from the best Greek writers that it is the office itself. Gill describes what made the office honourable and then declines to leave it there: the anointing, the garments, the maintenance, the retinue and the reverence shown were real enough, but the principal honour lay in the work, in representing the people, offering for them, blessing them and resolving their hard cases, in all of which they were types. Ellicott corrects the text of the second clause, so that it reads not "he that is called" but "when he is called." Barnes observes that Aaron was designated by name, so his successors required evidence as clear as if they too had been named, and that the law prescribing the succession was by then little regarded, the office having become venal and conferred at pleasure by the Roman authorities. Gill has the same complaint in his own words, that of late some had got into it of themselves. Robertson states the standard rather than the abuse, that the priest was called of God, which is the ideal and was true of Aaron.

What may be built on the verse divides them. Calvin takes the call of God as what makes any office lawful, notes that the two priesthoods share it while differing in that one was perpetual and the other therefore temporary, warns that Aaron's terms are not to be extended beyond what was decreed, and draws the general rule that no government may be set up in the church by the will of men. Clarke uses it to attack a doctrine rather than establish one, denying that the verse supports an unbroken succession of ordainers and that any such succession ever existed, and adding that even if it had it would be irrelevant, since the passage speaks only of an appointment within one tribe and family, that succession was itself broken, and the office was to cease with Christ, who can have no successor. Barnes draws the tightest limits of the group: the call meant is external rather than inward, and the verse has no reference to the Christian ministry and should not be applied to it. Robertson applies it anyway in a modified form, granting that the modern minister is not a priest but insisting he should be a God-called man rather than one who pushes himself into office. Wesley states the conclusion the chapter moves toward, that whatever is excellent in the older priesthood belongs to Christ more eminently and whatever is wanting in those priests is in him; he observes that Aaron did not preach at all, preaching being no part of the office.
5:
The claim is negative before it is positive: not that Christ seized the office but that he did not. Barnes reads it as a denial of ambition and explains why the denial was needed, since a man not descended from Aaron had to be shown to hold a regular vocation rather than to have intruded. Calvin fixes the verb, which here means to honour or magnify or exalt, and reduces the sentence to a single proposition, that Christ did not make himself a high priest but God made him one. Gill takes the making itself to have been a glorifying, though he distinguishes carefully: nothing can be added to the glory of the Son as God, and for him to become a priest at all was a condescension, so the honour belongs to the human nature that was united to him and separated to the office. Robertson notes that the verb of glorifying has to be supplied from the previous clause, and reports a difference among scholars on how the priesthood stands to the sonship, one holding the two coeval and another that the priesthood is merely fitting because he is Son; his own judgment is that the Father nominated him to it.

The first quotation is about sonship rather than priesthood, and Calvin admits the difficulty in his own words, that the passage may look far-fetched, since being begotten of God does not of itself make a man a priest. His answer is that the begetting the psalm speaks of was a testimony rendered before men, so the question becomes what sort of Son was manifested: not one endued with no honour or power, but one who was to stand between God and man, in which case the begetting included the priesthood. Ellicott resolves it more neatly through a single word. Where the Pentateuch gives the high priest a distinctive title it almost always calls him the anointed priest, so that in the one name "the Christ" both of the testimonies that follow are already joined, the Anointed King addressed as Son and the same figure addressed by the same voice as priest for ever. Barnes takes a lower road, noting that the language of the psalm is general enough to fit any exaltation conferred on the Redeemer and is used here with strict propriety. Wesley enters the one caution: the day named is not the moment of the appointment, the generation being from eternity.

On the second quotation they agree that everything later depends on it. Robertson calls it the crucial passage by which the superiority will be proved, notes that it says only "priest" where the argument wants "high priest" and that the writer treats the two as synonymous, and observes that at this stage the only point pressed is the divine appointment. Ellicott calls the verse the kernel of its psalm and the theme of a large part of the epistle, and suggests a preparation for it in the promise that Israel should be a kingdom of priests, the king being the type of the Son of David and the consecrated people dimly foreshadowing the Anointed Priest. Barnes assembles six reasons for referring the psalm to the Messiah, among them that David speaks of one superior whom he calls his Lord, that the figure addressed is expressly distinguished from the Lord himself, and that Jesus applied the words to himself. Calvin meets the counter-reading head on: those who apply it to David show extreme effrontery, since kings might not exercise the priesthood, and Uzziah was struck with leprosy for that one act of intermeddling. Clarke draws the practical conclusion he cares about, that a priest for ever admits no succession and can have no vicar, and Gill that the same speaker uttered both psalms. Of Melchizedek himself Clarke says only that who he was must remain a secret.
7:
Clarke concedes defeat in advance, calling this one of the most difficult places in the epistle if not in the whole New Testament, the labours of learned men upon it prodigious and their meaning hard to find even so. The phrase about the days of his flesh draws an identical defensive move from three of them independently. Calvin denies the word signifies anything material and makes it a condition instead, so that those who conclude the flesh has since been laid aside are raving; it is one thing to be a real man endued with blessed immortality, another to be liable to the sorrows Christ bore here. Gill says the same in plainer terms, that flesh was certainly his after the resurrection and only its infirmities are now gone, and Barnes that the human nature remains but is glorified. Robertson locates the scene without hesitation in Gethsemane, allowing that other occasions of weeping are in view but that this is chiefly meant. Gill lets the phrase cover the whole course of the earthly life, especially its later part, and Wesley narrows it hard, to the two days in which the suffering stood at its height.

Robertson supplies the word for supplication, formed from the noun for a suppliant and suggesting a man who comes carrying an olive branch; it appears nowhere else in the New Testament, though older writers pair it with the ordinary word for prayers as here. On being heard, the question is what was granted, since the death was not averted. Wesley answers it directly: he was heard, not so that the cup should pass, but so that he drank it. He goes further into what was dreaded, holding that the horror of a shameful death was not the worst of it but the weight of infinite justice, the being bruised by the hand of God himself, beside which all else was a mere nothing; and that throughout the life it was never the suffering but the dishonour done to God by sin that grieved that soul. Robertson reads the reverence named at the end as the attitude of one who surrendered his will at once and was thereby enabled to acquiesce. Ellicott notes that the clause about sonship may attach to this sentence, implying that the hearing was granted for the reverent fear and not because he was in the pre-eminent sense a Son.

That a Son should have to learn obedience is the sentence everybody stops at, and the guarding is careful. Barnes lists what cannot be meant: not that he was ignorant of obedience, not that he was indisposed to it, not that he had any perversity of nature needing to be subdued as ours does; what is meant is that he was willing to prove obedience in suffering. Calvin makes the same denial with a harder image, that he was not driven to it by force nor exercised as oxen and horses are when their ferocity is to be tamed, being already willing; yet he holds it may truly be said that by his death he learned what obeying costs, since he was then led in a special way to deny himself and to accept willingly a death he greatly dreaded. Robertson points out that the two verbs play on each other in the Greek, and says the Son always did his Father's will but grew in experience as in wisdom and stature. Ellicott quotes the distinction that the disposition existed before the suffering and that the passage from disposition to deed is what practical learning of a virtue means. Wesley thinks the clause interposed lest anyone be offended at so much human weakness, and notes that the word order shows how willingly the learning was done. Both Calvin and Barnes then turn it on the reader, agreeing that prosperity leaves us with loose reins and that affliction is what teaches submission.
9:
The participle rendered "made perfect" is read by nobody as moral improvement. Clarke takes it for having reached the goal and finished the labour, the same word used of the spirits of just men who have gained the prize, so that the course of suffering was completed by death and resurrection and the man was consecrated both priest and sacrifice at once by his offering. Barnes states the guard explicitly, that what was completed was fitness to be a Saviour and not moral perfection, since there was never any sin. Robertson calls it the finishing of a training carried on by means of sufferings, and Gill the completing of an obedience. Calvin prefers "consecrated" outright, granting that the Greek will bear either but arguing that where the subject is priesthood the language of sanctification is what fits, and citing the words spoken in the upper room about sanctifying himself for their sakes; he adds that the term applies properly to the human nature, in which the priestly office was discharged and the suffering borne. Ellicott makes the whole process the manner in which the one who glorified him to be high priest brought him into possession of the office.

The qualifying clause about obeying him produces the chapter's flattest contradiction. Clarke takes it as decisive against a doctrine: he tasted death for every man but is the author of eternal salvation only to those who obey, so it is not believers but obedient believers who are finally saved, which he calls unimpeachable evidence that no man is saved by an obedience of Christ's reckoned to him. Calvin argues the opposite from the same verse, insisting the writer does not offer Christ merely as an example but ascends higher, to an obedience that blotted out our transgressions and obtained righteousness for us before God, the disobedience of Adam being removed by an act of the contrary kind. Neither is hedging and neither mentions the other. The rest keep to the middle. Clarke passes on a threefold summary that obedience is as necessary to salvation as believing, that the perfecting was by the offering of himself, and that pardon was obtained by that merit for those who obey; Barnes says only that this is not to save those who live in sin and that obedience is the sole evidence anyone has; Wesley glosses obeying as doing and suffering his whole will, and Ellicott finds a model of obedience presented to all.

The verb closing the paragraph is not the ordinary word for appointing, and they take pains over it. Robertson notes it means to salute or address, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is common in Plutarch; Ellicott renders it "addressed" rather than "called"; Barnes insists it does not say the man was appointed to the office at all, only that he was so addressed, namely in the psalm; Wesley says it properly means surnamed. Clarke supplies the flavour from an old lexicon that glosses it as saluting, in the way that those who accosted a newly made king would hail him as king. Ellicott observes what the quotation does with its source, that where the psalm said priest the text now says high priest, and that the change is what brings the psalm's meaning fully out; Barnes replies that the Hebrew word covers both and that nothing in the argument turns on which is used. Gill lists the points of likeness that make the order fit, the absence of recorded parentage, the manner of the instalment, and the antiquity and perpetuity of the office. Wesley suspects the concealment of who Melchizedek was to have been deliberate, so that he might be the more eminent type. Henry reports the view that the things hard to be uttered concern not that figure but the one he prefigured.
11:
What the many things concern is disputed. Clarke lists three candidates, Melchizedek, Christ, and the endless priesthood, and argues against the first on a practical ground: the seventh chapter says a great deal more about that figure and says it plainly, and the readers could hardly have grown more capable in the few hours between the writing of the two. He settles on the priesthood, which he thinks carnal Christians cannot easily grasp. Robertson makes it the likeness between the two priesthoods and notes the pronoun could be either masculine or neuter; Ellicott reads it of the whole subject; Gill declines to choose and allows all of them. On the adjective they agree against the familiar rendering. It means hard to interpret rather than hard to utter, as Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson each say, Robertson adding that the word is a rare compound found in two Greek authors and nowhere else in the New Testament. Where the difficulty lies is a separate question, and Calvin answers it flatly: not in the subject but in the hearers, since the Lord speaks so clearly that his word is called our light, and it is our darkness that dims the brightness. Wesley says the same more briefly.

The word for dullness is built on a negative and a verb meaning to push, which Robertson renders as no push in the hearing, sluggish in the mind as much as in the ears, and notes that Plato used it of stupid students. Clarke takes it of a man who walks heavily and makes little speed, elegantly chosen for people summoned to a race with the road laid plain before them. Calvin distinguishes two senses and picks the harder: dull in the ears would mean inattentive, but sluggish in the ears means slowness of comprehension. Ellicott suggests the faculty had once been acute, so that few words would then have sufficed, and that what has come upon them since is a lack of interest bringing a want of power. Barnes admits nobody can now recover what particular fact grounded the charge. On their being fit to teach by now, Gill counts the advantages: descent from Abraham, the law and the writings, sometimes the ministry of Christ or his apostles, and thirty years since Pentecost. Barnes infers from the verse that these were not recent converts, and reads the expectation modestly, not that all should preach but that all should be able to explain the faith to a child or a neighbour.

Calvin reduces the reproof to a sentence, that they do not know the alphabet, and then guards it: we must indeed go on learning all our lives, since only the man who owns himself far from perfect knowledge is truly wise, but we ought to profit enough not to remain always among the first principles. He adds that not years only but days must be accounted for. Clarke corrects the grammar, the pronoun being accusative rather than nominative, so that someone must teach them a second time certain elements; and he reads the words as implying they had once been better taught and had forgotten, having probably given up hearing the gospel, which is why the letter was written. On what the oracles are, Ellicott finds good reason from the usage of the New Testament and of Philo for taking them as the Old Testament scriptures, and Clarke says the same; Barnes allows either that or everything God had then revealed. Robertson notes that the noun is a diminutive, divine utterances being usually brief. The figure of milk Clarke traces through authors sacred and profane who use it of first principles and speak of sucking for learning; Robertson explains it by the want of intellectual and spiritual teeth. Henry states the principle underneath the rebuke, that dull hearers make preaching difficult and that much is looked for from those to whom much is given.
13:
Ellicott notices a shift the English hides: the complaint has moved from needing milk to living on it, making it the sole food by choice, so that the readers stand self-confessed as infants. He guesses at what lay behind it, a temptation to mix rudimentary Christian teaching with that of the synagogue, and warns that yielding would have cost them the elements of Christian truth and any real grasp of the older scriptures besides. Calvin reads the infancy as one of understanding rather than of standing, and puts it in a phrase, that it constrains God to prattle with us; he adds that a grown man is not averse to milk, only to living on nothing else, which is exactly Wesley's qualification. Gill has the same double reading, of one who sits down contented with first principles or who uses the ceremonial law as a schoolmaster. On the adjective they agree: it means inexperienced rather than unskilful, and Robertson derives it from the word for a trial while Barnes is careful to add that it does not question whether these were Christians at all, only whether they had the experience to take in the higher matters.

What "the word of righteousness" means then divides them four ways, and two of them contradict each other outright. Clarke takes it for the doctrine of justification and says he believes this to be the writer's meaning, so that the man who lives on milk is one who rests in the ceremonies of the law and is inexperienced in justification, which requires faith in the sacrificial death. Calvin denies precisely that: the apostle, as he thinks, is not raising the question how we are justified before God at all, but using the word in a simpler sense for the completeness of knowledge that leads on to maturity. Wesley turns the phrase against the very doctrine Clarke finds in it, glossing it as the sublimer truths of the gospel and identifying the milk-fed with those who desire and can digest nothing but justification and imputed righteousness. Barnes stays with Clarke's sense, the doctrine of how men become righteous. Ellicott declines all of these and takes it for properly developed Christian teaching as such, though he admits the choice of word needs explaining, righteousness not being this epistle's manifest subject, and looks for the explanation in the writer's general kinship with Paul. Robertson ventures only that moral truth is perhaps meant.

On those of full age Gill is the most careful. The perfection meant is not of justification, since babes in Christ are as perfectly justified as the grown; nor of sanctification, there being no perfect holiness in this life; nor of parts, which infants have as truly as adults; it is a perfection of knowledge, some having come further into the mysteries than others. Robertson makes the same distinction in one word, calling it relative rather than absolute perfection. Clarke lists what the solid food consists of: the atonement, justification by faith, the gift of the Spirit, triumph over death, the glorification of body and soul. The clause about use draws out the best of them. Barnes insists the figure is not of eaters learning to tell good food from bad but of experienced Christians telling useful teaching from injurious, a delicate taste for the doctrines that impart light. Calvin makes the point defensively, that we cannot be rightly taught unless fortified against Satan's delusions, since a faith suspended between truth and falsehood may come to nothing at any moment. Robertson notes that the word for senses is the Stoics' term for the organs of perception and that an ancient physician uses the very phrase found here; Clarke enumerates the organs and adds that something in the soul answers to each. Wesley takes the habit to be strength of understanding arising from maturity, by which such men exercise themselves with ease and cheerfulness.
